title: Bluesky’s AI assistant Attie expands into an open social research tool
teaser: Bluesky’s AI tool expands its reach via 'Quests,' allowing users to research information across the entire open web (AT Protocol).
summary: Bluesky's AI assistant, Attie, is expanding its utility by introducing 'Quests,' a new feature that transforms it into an open research tool. Quests allows users to query and research information and news spanning the entire open social web, which includes all apps utilizing the underlying AT Protocol, not just Bluesky. Bluesky states this tool aims to empower users to 'find the truth' and combat misinformation. While the platform reported a slowdown in growth, the company remains focused on monetization and expanding services. The shift is supported by $100 million raised in a 2025 funding round, giving the company runway to develop tools like Attie, which is currently in beta.
author: Sarah Perez
content: Attie , Bluesky's AI assistant that lets you build custom social feeds without programming, is evolving into an open-ended research tool. The company this week said it's added a new feature to the AI assistant, called Quests, that lets users ask it for information and news spreading across the broader Bluesky social network, nicknamed the Atmosphere. This includes not only Bluesky, but also any app that integrates with the underlying AT Protocol. Bluesky's user growth has slowed over the past eight months - the social network saw its user base double to 40 million last October, within just a year, but it now reports around 45.6 million registered accounts . So the company has been looking to develop tools and services that could allow it to grow its user base and potentially monetize it. Attie, launched in March , is a separate product by Bluesky that lets users design their own algorithm, create custom feeds, and, one day possibly, vibe-code their own apps. While the AI assistant is free for the time being, the company has toyed with the idea of charging for the service. Quests adds new capabilities to Attie, allowing users to ask it open-ended questions to research what's happening on this part of the open social web. For instance, you could ask Attie to pull information about trending topics, or help you identify the most influential accounts in a particular field or location, the company explained. Image Credits: Bluesky (screenshot) "Attie's AI is a tool that helps you make sense of the internet, helping you fight back against the proliferation of misinformation and noise by giving you the tools to find the truth yourself," wrote Bluesky's chief innovation officer Jay Graber, who stepped down in March from her role as CEO of the company . (She's since been replaced by Toni Schneider, the former founding CEO of Automattic.) "Our bet is that tools that help people make sense of the world will prove to be more useful than those that fill it with confusion," Graber wrote. "We want Attie to reduce the barrier to entry and expertise required to learn how to use the AT Protocol, and to put the tools for customizing your experience in the hands of anyone who wants them." Graber noted Attie is being redesigned to add accessibility features and a new logo, and more changes are coming in the months ahead. For now, the new Attie experience is in beta, and users will be invited in from a waitlist over the coming weeks. While many Bluesky users tend to dislike AI for economic, political, and environmental reasons, the company has had to balance its community's leanings with the need to generate revenue to help itself and the AT Protocol development it leads remain afloat. In March, Bluesky said it had raised $100 million in funding in a round that closed in 2025. That gives it runway to experiment with ideas like Attie and how AI can play a role in the Atmosphere, as well as with other services, like a premium subscription or tools for power users.

title: Rivian sues the US government for ‘full refund’ of Trump tariffs
teaser: Rivian sues the U.S. government seeking a full refund of tariffs paid under 'Liberation Day' taxes after the Supreme Court ruled the tariffs unconstitutional.
summary: Automaker Rivian has filed a lawsuit against the U.S. government, naming U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) as a defendant, to recover tariffs paid under the Trump administration's 'Liberation Day' taxes. The company seeks a 'full refund' and wants the trade court to declare the tariffs 'contrary to law.' Although the Supreme Court invalidated the tariffs, Rivian's lawyers argue a separate action is necessary because importers are not guaranteed a refund of previously paid amounts. The lawsuit comes as Rivian prepares to launch its mass-market R2 SUV and continues to raise capital, recently selling shares to raise $1.3 billion. The tariffs were originally justified under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).
author: Sean O'Kane
content: Rivian has filed a lawsuit against the U.S. government in an attempt to claw back a "full refund" on tariffs it paid under President Trump's "Liberation Day" taxes, which the Supreme Court later ruled unconstitutional. The automaker joins a long line of companies seeking such refunds. In April, Rivian CFO Claire McDonough said she expected the company stood to reap a refund in the "tens of millions of dollars." Rivian's action comes as the company is in the middle of rolling out its first mass-market SUV, the R2. It expects to ship around 20,000 to 25,000 of them by the end of this year and help the company finally reach profitability. Reaching that goal may not happen until 2028 , though, as Rivian is currently plowing a lot of money into developing autonomous vehicles. The company recently sold shares to raise around $1.3 billion to help pad out its cash balance in the meantime. The lawsuit, filed on Thursday in the U.S. Court of International Trade, names the U.S. government, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), and CBP's commissioner Rodney Scott as defendants. CBP collected the tariffs on behalf of the Trump administration, which tried to justify them under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). In a statement to TechCrunch, CBP said that over $121  billion in both "potential and certified refunds have been accepted for processing ." The agency did not comment specifically on the lawsuit. Earlier this month, the Cato Institute wrote that $71 billion had been paid out, which "suggests that frictions built into" the refund process created "obstacles for importers seeking refunds." According to Rivian's lawsuit, the company wants a guarantee that it will get its money - and the proper amount - back from the government. "Although the Supreme Court invalidated the tariffs, this separate action remains necessary because importers that have paid IEEPA tariffs, including Plaintiffs, are not guaranteed a refund of amounts previously paid based on the Supreme Court's decision," Rivian's lawyers wrote in the complaint. Rivian did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe told Reuters last year after the tariffs were imposed that he expected the cost of each vehicle to rise by "a couple of thousand dollars" as a result. By the end of 2025, he said the company had mitigated the impact to "low hundreds of dollars." "The resulting environment of retaliatory trade or other practices or additional trade restrictions or barriers has harmed, and could continue to harm, our ability to obtain necessary raw materials, components and equipment and could harm our ability to sell our products and services at prices customers are willing to pay," the company wrote in a regulatory filing earlier this year. Rivian is asking the trade court to declare the tariffs "contrary to law," issue a refund with interest, and pay any associated court fees.

title: Dev accidentally commits Copilot binary to FreeBSD ports repo
teaser: Accidental Copilot commit forces FreeBSD repo freeze; developers are flocking to simpler VCS alternatives like Game of Trees (Got) to escape Git's complexity.
summary:
The FreeBSD ports repository recently faced a technical hiccup when a developer accidentally committed a Copilot binary, forcing a repository freeze. This occurred because GitHub's mirroring limit is 100 MiB, unable to handle the file size, though the package itself is not meant to include the proprietary binary.

Beyond this incident, the article explores the widespread developer frustration with the complexity of Git. As developers seek simpler tools, several Git-compatible alternatives have emerged. These include Game of Trees (Got), a system from OpenBSD that prioritizes ease of use, and other options like Jujutsu (Jj) and Gitless. While these alternatives exist, they often require users to already be knowledgeable about complex version control concepts.
content: OS PLATFORMS Dev accidentally commits Copilot binary to FreeBSD ports repo Git is aptly named: it isn't easy - but there are alternatives The FreeBSD project froze its ports repository on Wednesday. The reason turns out to be a slightly embarrassing Git-related oopsie where a version of Copilot got uploaded somewhere it should not have been. The announcement of the 2026 Ports Repository Freeze went out on July 21 and remained in effect the following day, as explained in a message on the freebsd-announce mailing list . The mail delicately skirted around exactly what happened: « The commit in question severed our ports tree mirroring to github.com due to their filesize hard limit of 100MB, and introduced a blob of questionable licensing into the repository history. » The offending commit is this one . An accidental, but amusing, commit to FreeBSD's ports repository - an entire Microsoft LLM Liam Proven It's not a disaster; the problem is that the Ports repository is automatically mirrored to various places, including a read-only Github mirror - and as Github's docs say , "GitHub blocks files larger than 100 MiB." There is already an official FreeBSD port of Copilot , but FreeBSD terminology is slightly confusing here: the "port" is effectively a sort of package that allows the Linux binary to run inside FreeBSD's Linux emulation, called the Linuxulator . It isn't a native FreeBSD version of Copilot, and the package is not meant to include the actual Copilot CLI binary - partly because that is under its own custom license . That's what FreeBSD's Kyle Evans meant by "questionable licensing". We don't blame anyone for using any available resources to help with using GitHub. Navigating Linux, FreeBSD, and worst of all Git is hard, especially the last one. Git is aptly named - it's not an acronym, it's a real word : someone annoying or unpleasant. It is, however, now more or less the de facto standard version control system of the FOSS world. Despite not being a developer, the Reg FOSS desk worked with Git on a daily basis for over four years - blame the Docs as Code philosophy - and developed a deep and abiding dislike for it. It's not just us: it's in an XKCD comic , so it must be true. (This vulture has directly lived the experience described in that comic.) Personally, we always found Git much harder work than the tar command . It should come as no surprise that multiple teams are working on compatible alternatives. A Game of Thrones Trees Just the day before some FreeBSD developer's regrettably public mishap, a new version of one of those alternatives appeared: Game of Trees version 0.127 . Game of Trees , known as Got for short, is a Git-compatible version control system (VCS) developed by contributors to the OpenBSD Project. It's been in development since 2019 , and we feel that the project has a nice line in self-deprecation - starting with the homepage's project description: "a version control system which prioritizes ease of use and simplicity over flexibility." This is, we suspect, in response to Git's self-description , which says that it is "designed to handle everything from small to very large projects with speed and efficiency." We also like the Got project goals and especially the FAQ , which really does not beat about the bush: « Does Got aim to replace Git? No. Got does not aim to replace Git. Got can be used instead of Git (for some tasks), or in addition to Git. If you are already using Git and are happy with it, you don't need Got. » And even more succinctly, under the anchor "pointless" : « What's the point of all this? Why not just use Git? If you are wondering why Got even exists, you can just ignore it. » Got isn't the only tool that aims to remain compatible with Git, but simplify the experience. Gitless is another, which describes itself as "a simple version control system built on top of Git," and says that it's "easy to learn and use." Unfortunately, development seems to have gone quiet: the last release appeared the same year that Got appeared. Another (and even younger) Git-compatible VCS is Jujutsu , often called just "Jj", and not to be confused with the traditional Japanese martial art Jiu Jitsu . Jujutsu the VCS has lots of documentation , but if it has a weakness, it's that it rather assumes that you already know your way around VCS use in general and Git in particular. If that's not the case for you, you might find Jujutsu for Everyone by Remo Senekowitsch more helpful. ®

title: Nothing confirms layoffs, but calls market exit rumors ‘fake news’
teaser: Facing layoff rumors, a tech company announced it is reorganizing around a new AI-native unit, while reporting record sales of 29,537 units.
summary: A company issued a statement aggressively debunking rumors of market exits and major layoffs. Instead, the firm announced a strategic reorganization to fuel future growth, focusing on efficiency and advanced technology. Key initiatives include creating dedicated business units, notably an AI-native unit, and consolidating country operations into regional hubs. The company emphasized that while some positions were affected—admitting to minor staff changes—the reports of mass layoffs are 'way overblown.' The firm reassured stakeholders, pointing to the Phone 4b's record-breaking first-day sales of 29,537 units as evidence of its market strength, framing the changes as necessary steps for the next era of personal computing.
author: Stevie Bonifield
content: FAKE NEWS... We are not shutting down any markets. Inaccurate reports are being circulated; Phone (4b) sold 29,537 units on Day 1 only, breaking records in its price segment. What we are doing is reorganising our teams to prepare for our next phase of growth. We are introducing dedicated business units - including an AI-native business unit - and consolidating individual countries into regional hubs to operate much more efficiently. These changes have impacted certain positions, and while we are unable to share specific details due to regulatory compliance and ongoing local consultation processes, the reported numbers are way overblown, and we call on the media to uphold factual reporting and journalistic integrity. Decisions that impact people's livelihoods are never taken lightly, and we know how difficult this transition is for our team members who are affected. We are deeply grateful for their contributions and are fully committed to supporting them through this process. While these are hard decisions, it is a necessary step to position us to shape the next era of personal computing.
